name: Gareth Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead guitar sessions for a small recording house, write short cues, meaning bits of music timed to a film, and teach on two evenings. I have a master’s in music and I am good at fixing a take when the picture changes, but this town pays less than a senior player expects.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has to line up outside the studio?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I trade pickup for our two school-age children. We have a mortgage and about three weeks of household expenses saved, so a late invoice is felt at our kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the recording house that faster invoices are welcome, but the guitarist still has to find the right sound. I would keep the paid sessions and my evening pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An ordinary late payment is enough to make us tense with only three weeks saved. A plateau would leave our work mostly alone, yet it would not make the studio pay on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would keep playing paid cues and teaching the eight evening pupils. I would ask the producer to put the next invoice date and late-payment rule in writing before delivering another film cue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about cash arriving after the mortgage date. I am not expecting AI to take the chair in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When was the last late invoice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A travel advert took six weeks longer than agreed to pay. We postponed replacing the children’s worn school shoes until it cleared, and I would chase the next invoice on its written due date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI on those cues now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only now and then for a rough timing list. I still watch the film and check every cue point myself before playing.

I would ask for a **written due date** before delivering another cue.
think: Our **three-week reserve** makes delayed studio pay a direct problem for the next mortgage instalment.

do: Keep **paid film cues** and eight evening pupils this week.
Request a **written invoice date** and chase late pay on that date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing late payments and a thin reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the producer that software may cut a rough film cue quickly, but a final guitar take still needs ears. I would ask which studio hours are actually paid before holding an evening free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cues and edits make up about a third of my pay, and cheap generated music could take many of them. The eight pupils help, but a teaching evening does not replace a studio week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask the producer for written paid session hours and a demonstration of the studio’s new cue checker. In the first year I would test it only after the engineer gives me paid instruction and approves local storage, using my own nameless guitar take; I would compare each suggested cue by ear against the film and stop if timing is wrong or a file leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing sessions. A clever cue checker cannot sign the household mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put a pupil’s recording into the checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A child’s voice and name stay outside a tool without school permission and a storage rule; my own take will do for a test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a different studio seat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if my paid hours really fall. There are few local openings, and I would apply only for a posted paid guitarist job whose written net pay after travel and pickup hours beat the lost sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the studio that AGI by 2028 can make whole film cues for less than a session fee. I would ask for signed work orders rather than a promise of calls next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most cue-writing fees to end in 2028 and some paid guitar sessions to disappear with them. Robots that can play physically arrive around 2031, three years later, but an electronic soundtrack can leave me unpaid before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total the cue invoices and ask for signed paid session dates. In the first year after 2028, if studio playing hours also fall, I would apply for a posted arts-centre guitar tutor role only if my master’s degree qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces the lost sessions and pickup works; I would keep the eight pupils and paid studio work until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed because cues and sessions together are most of my own pay. I lie awake deciding which mortgage bill a three-week reserve could actually cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unfunded teacher course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take only a funded place or paid study time if the actual posted tutor role requires that certificate. Tuition cannot come out of three weeks of mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the arts centre mentions a possible job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a posting and written hours. I cannot exchange a paid studio call for a rumour.

Keep **pupils and sessions** until a suitable written offer is signed.

S2.quote: I cannot exchange a paid studio call for a rumour.
fieldNote: His **2028 cue loss** precedes capable playing robots around 2031.
The **tutor move** needs actual paid hour cuts, a posted qualified role, written net pay, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Apply for qualified posted tutor after 2028 cuts; written net after travel replaces sessions, pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the producer that five years until AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn another paid craft. I would look at sound editing for live venues, where someone still has to hear the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Film cues may stop paying by 2031, and playing robots could follow around 2034. A venue sound role might work, but a certificate without a vacancy would only add a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would take a six-month venue sound course only if the local centre gives me a funded place, paid training hours and a schedule that fits pickup without cutting my partner’s wages. In the first year after 2031, if studio fees fall, I would apply for a posted paid venue sound role only if the certificate qualifies me, its written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and pickup works; I would keep pupils and paid studio calls until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the recording income, though a funded course gives me a route. I will not pay tuition just to feel busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you practise on a live show without supervision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The venue technician would supervise the first sound checks, and I would not handle a crowded show alone until the equipment and safety checks are signed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course offers funding but no paid hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep the paid studio shifts and ask for another intake. Free tuition does not replace the wages I lose during training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the studio team that ten years until AGI by 2036 gives us time to insist on paid credits and keep learning. A credit does not buy groceries if the session fee is missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cue fees may disappear by 2036 and playing robots may reach venues around 2039. My problem is also immediate: three weeks of savings will not carry a family through a slow winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I would put five percent of every extra paid lesson fee aside after food, mortgage and school costs, aiming for three months while asking the studio for written minimum session fees. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid lessons and sessions, and apply for a posted music-centre production lead role only if my degree qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost sessions and pickup works; I would leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about both the current reserve and later cue losses. Ten years helps with planning but not with this month’s due date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no extra pupils book, what do you save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new from lessons that week. I cannot count a fee before a pupil pays it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a title make you leave the studio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a real posting and written net pay that covers the sessions I lose. I will not give up a paid call for a senior-sounding label.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue and session fees could go before I have a reserve. Signed studio work, a real qualified tutor opening and pickup that does not eat another wage would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask when the invoice lands. A recording credit looks fine on a screen, but our lender takes money, not applause.

headlineQuote: A recording credit looks fine on a screen, but our lender takes money, not applause.
portrait: At **43**, Gareth leads guitar sessions, writes film cues and teaches eight pupils with a music master’s degree.
His **lower pay**, three-week reserve, mortgage and few local jobs make late invoices a serious risk.
He tests a **new cue checker** only after paid instruction, approved storage and listening against the film.
A **funded sound course** would need paid hours and child pickup without reducing his partner’s wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove cue fees and paid guitar sessions before he builds a reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed studio work**, a qualified paid tutor vacancy and pickup without another lost wage would help Gareth.
